<reason>CON built one coherent indictment—the "materially affects" qualifier is unlocatable before litigation—and defended it through every round. PRO's flashiest move (flipping CON's adviser/foreman/hospital examples as proof the standard works) was substantially neutralized by CON's proof-timing response: those harms are real on day one but provable only after discovery into clients' unstated motives, so employers must act on risk while the law permits action only on litigable proof. PRO never answered that burden. Under pressure, PRO's A1 introduced "reasonable, good-faith business judgment," which CON convincingly framed as a reasonableness amendment the motion's objective text doesn't contain—"a draft, not a standard"—and PRO's closing never addressed this charge or the motive-audit vs. world-audit distinction, instead repeating that CON offered "no method," a claim the record contradicts (CON repeatedly named enumerated ex ante statutes). PRO's values case (asymmetry, chilling effects, patchwork gaps) stayed morally compelling and its openings/rebuttals were strong, which keeps this competitive, but on the decision-relevant clash—does the standard work as written—CON controlled the back half of the debate and crystallized it cleanly in the closing.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's Rebuttal 2: A1 distinguishing motive-review (employer's own records) from caused-harm review (discovery into third parties' psychology)—"one audits the decision-maker; the other audits the world"—answered PRO's sharpest pressure question and went unrebutted, and A4.5 converted PRO's good-faith answer into the decisive "rewritten mid-debate" frame.</best_rebuttal>
